body_markdown:
A California car enthusiast and a storied design studio have joined forces to create the first “new” Studebaker in more than 60 years, relying on sketches by one of the 20th century’s most prolific designers. It’s been a winding road to get to this point, though, and a bit of backstory is in order.


Studebaker stopped U.S. production of passenger cars and light trucks in 1964, but the corporation’s automotive division had been financially circling the drain throughout the previous decade. High labor costs; old and inefficient factories; the cost of developing, in-house, a modern high-compression OHV V-8 engine; intense competition from the Big Three domestic automakers; quality control issues; aging platforms; and a fiscally disastrous merger with Packard made Studebaker’s demise as a car company just about inevitable.


Entering the 1960s, Studebaker’s managers in South Bend did what they could do to keep the company afloat. The introduction of the compact Lark briefly raised prospects, but the Big Three responded to the success of the Lark (and American Motors’ little Rambler) with their own compact cars, like the Ford Falcon, Chevrolet Corvair, Pontiac Tempest, and the Mopar Dart/Valiant. Studebaker also introduced the sporting, fiberglass-bodied Avanti, styled by Raymond Loewy’s studio, to compete with the Corvette. Tuned by Andy Granatelli, the Avanti set land-speed records for production cars and gained Studebaker considerable publicity but few sales.


1953 Starliner Coupe


Studebaker


Another South Bend salvo from Loewy’s studio had shown up earlier, in 1953. He and his team had been working for Studebaker since the 1930s, and the ’53 Starliner coupe, penned by Loewy designer Bob Bourke, is considered to be one of the most beautiful cars ever made. For the 1956 model year, Bourke used the Starliner’s shell to create the Hawk, Studebaker’s flagship luxury model. The original Hawks were stylistically of their era and not unattractive, something that can’t be said for the “Packardbaker” versions made following the merger, which some folks think rank among the ugliest production automobiles extant.


1956 Golden Hawk


Tony Bock/Toronto Star/Getty Images


Tony Bock/Toronto Star/Getty Images


Said Bourke about those unfortunate Hawks, “I kept it restrained as possible, and after I left Studebaker, it really got out of hand with the wild fins, Mylar overlays, yards of chrome, and complete lack of restraint.”


By the 1960s, though, the winds of fresh, new design themes were blowing across Detroit. Studebaker responded by hiring independent stylist Brooks Stevens to update the Hawk for the 1962 model year.


[Clifford Brooks Stevens](https://mam.org/collection/archives/brooks-stevens/) (1911–95) was an American industrial designer whose studio was responsible for more than 3000 design commissions, including vehicles, household appliances, packaging, graphics, logos, and more.


1949 Harley-Davidson FL Hydra-Glide


Mecum


He styled the 1949 Harley-Davidson Hydra-Glide, which influenced motorcycle design for decades, along with the 1948 Willys Jeepster, another monumental design. He also did notable work for Lawn-Boy, Briggs & Stratton, and Evinrude/Johnson outboard motors and boats.


1948 Willys Jeepster


National Motor Museum/Heritage Images/Getty Images


Stevens is credited with designing the[first motorhome](https://www.hemmings.com/stories/this-officer-is-not-a-truck-it-is-a-housecar-the-incomplete-history-of-the-brooks-stevens-motorhomes/) , as well as a side-by-side[snowmobile “coupe” concept](http://davidsleds2.mysite.com/PAGE_22850.html) with bucket seats and a steering wheel, for Evinrude. Stevens’ studio was also responsible for the Miller High Life logo and the 1958 iteration of the Oscar Mayer Wienermobile.


Evinrude


Oscar Mayer


For Studebaker, Stevens removed the fins and other garish ornamentation from the Hawk. He bladed the fenders, reduced the 1950s-style side cove to just a character line, and gave the car a squared-off, faux targa along with a formal roofline. The result was something that didn’t look out of place or dated next to a 1961 Lincoln Continental—quite an accomplishment when you consider it was based on a body shell first designed in the early 1950s.


Stevens’ GT Hawk certainly met with Bob Bourke’s approval. “It was not until 1962, when Brooks Stevens began to clean the basic body buck up again with his GT Hawks, that the car started to look right again. In my opinion, the best-looking Hawk made after 1956 was the last one, made in 1964,” Bourke said.


Brooks Stevens and the Studebaker GT Hawk.


Brooks Stevens, Inc.


As mentioned, Studebaker managers continued to come up with ideas even as the company was failing. If you visit the Studebaker National Museum in South Bend, Indiana, on the third floor you can see the Stevens-designed Sceptre, a full-size prototype for a grand-touring coupe intended to replace the Hawk in the 1966 model year. Also present are notchback and four-door Avanti proposals by the Loewy studio.


Studebaker Sceptre Concept


[Ronnie Schreiber](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rschreiber/)


Although the Sceptre and Loewy concepts are fairly well known to car enthusiasts in general and Studebaker fans in particular, less well known is the fact that Stevens had drawn an updated version of his GT Hawk proposed for the 1965 model year. The design removed remaining vestiges of 1950s elements, with particular restyling of the grille and front end and a reshaping of the rear decklid, to give the car an even more contemporary look. Unfortunately, Studebaker stopped U.S. production in 1964 (limping along with Canadian and complete knock-down kit assembly in Israel and South America until 1966), and Stevens’ 1965 GT Hawk never got beyond the drawing board.


Enter Don Lace, Jr. Along with his brother Jeff, Don runs[Lace Music Products](https://lacemusic.com/) . Unless you’re into guitars, that name may not be familiar to you, but you are probably familiar with the fruit of their work. Lace Music makes guitar pickups in Southern California, and the brothers’ father, Don Lace, Sr., founded a company called Actodyne General to make solenoids, which require coils of copper wire. He started working with Don Randall, who had been president and general manager of Fender Musical Instruments prior to founding the Randall amplifier company. The senior Lace consulted with Randall on the forming and winding of loudspeaker coils. That relationship led to Don Sr.’s development of the Lace Sensor guitar pickup, used by notable guitar players such as Eric Clapton, Jeff Beck, Buddy Guy, Pete Townshend, James Burton, Billy Corgan, Richie Blackmore, and Jack White. Entering the 21st century, Lace patented and introduced the revolutionary “Alumitone” line of pickups, which have a wider, flatter frequency response than conventional pickups, while using 90% less copper in their coils for greater sustainability. ( *Disclosure: Lace Music helps make the custom Alumitone pickups for the[Harmonicaster](http://www.harmonicaster.com/) electric harmonica that author Ronnie Schreiber invented and developed.* — *Ed.* )


Jeff Beck playing his signature Fender Stratocaster with Lace Sensor pickups.


David Redfern/Redferns


The association between popular music and cars is well-established. Cars have been a theme of popular music going back to “[In My Merry Oldsmobile](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y7QnPtkn8q0) ,” and many musicians, from The Jazz Singer’s[Al Jolson](https://rmsothebys.com/auctions/sj11/lots/r170-1932-packard-906-individual-custom-twin-six-convertible-sedan-by-dietrich/) to Pink Floyd’s **[Nick Mason](https://www.forbes.com/sites/peterlyon/2025/03/24/pink-floyds-nick-mason-has-a-car-collection-to-die-for/) have had an appreciation for fine automobiles. “Cars & Guitars” is a staple theme in the museum industry. The Lace brothers are no exception to that association, and they inherited automotive enthusiasm from Don Sr., who had a supercharged 1937 Cord.


Jeff Lace is currently restomodding a ’48 Packard that is sitting in a tent outside their small factory in Orange County, waiting for the hidden headlights from a ’42 DeSoto to be grafted on. His brother is more into classics than customs. Like their father, Don Jr. likes Cords and has even owned one of[Glenn Pray’s continuation Cords](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/glenn-pray-lost-everything-to-keep-auburns-and-cords-alive/) , but his real passion is for Studebakers, and he’s particularly fond of the Hawk. “I’ve had a Hawk in my life for 50 years,” he told me, and he has owned five GT Hawks over the years, including a high-performance R1 version, a two-owner California car that’s been retrofitted with a hi-po 283-cubic-inch small-block Chevy V-8.


Don Lace Jr’s Studebaker R1 GT Hawk


[Ronnie Schreiber](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rschreiber/)


At some point, Don Jr. came across Stevens’ sketches for the proposed 1965 GT Hawk. In the early 1990s, he wrote a letter to the designer, then in his 80s, about the ’65 proposal, saying that he wanted to bring it to life. A week later, he got a phone call from Stevens to discuss the project, and the men established a cordial relationship. However, Brooks Stevens passed away in 1995, and the project never went anywhere.


After Brooks Stevens retired, his son Kipp Stevens managed the Brooks Stevens Design firm in Milwaukee, until it was purchased by Ingenium Product Development in 2007. Under Ingenium, the agency focused more on engineering. In 2020, Brooks Stevens Design was purchased by Mark McAllister and current company president Michael Hopkins. The new leadership team says their approach is to look to the future while honoring the past, emphasizing the agency’s design expertise.


Brooks Stevens’ 1965 Studebaker GT Hawk Proposal


Brooks Stevens, Inc.


About five or six years ago, Don Jr.’s phone at Lace Music rang, with “Brooks Stevens” on the caller ID. One of the studio’s carbon-fiber fabricators was building a guitar and wanted some information about pickups. That inspired Don Jr. to dig up his old correspondence with Stevens, and he decided to make a proposal to the studio’s owners to commission a build of the designer’s ’65 GT Hawk, based on his own R1. The timing was fortuitous, as the company had recently changed hands and new management saw the project as a perfect fit for the firm’s renewed focus on vision and creativity.


Brooks Stevens, Inc.


Lace shipped his R1 GT Hawk to Milwaukee, where it was 3D scanned. Brooks Stevens’ revised body panels were rendered digitally and combined with the scans to create a 3D-printed physical model about the size of a shoebox for Don Jr. to review. Don gave his approval, and the project got underway.


Brooks Stevens, Inc.


I spoke to Ryan Hahn, former head of styling for Buell motorcycles and current design director at Brooks Stevens Design, about the effort. He said that when Lace approached them, they went back to Stevens’ original journal entries, where he laid out the business plan for a revised ’65 GT Hawk, including Studebaker’s limited financial resources and how consumer tastes were changing. The journal included some possible variations, including convertible and removable targa-topped versions.


Hahn said they hope to start the first build sometime this year. Original plans were to take commissions on six cars, but there appears to be some demand, as the[project’s website](https://www.65hawk.com/) now says that a dozen cars will be built. There is some thought of doing a targa version and possibly a period-authentic race car.


Brooks Stevens, Inc.


The plan is to use existing GT Hawks as donor cars, with Lace’s R1 as the prototype, and retain the original Studebaker VINs. That will keep things legal in terms of the EPA, DOT, and Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards. Some limited-run tooling will need to be made for forming the new hood, fascia, decklid, and grille. While some of the build will be done in-house with their own CNC and rapid prototyping gear, the studio’s core competencies are in design and engineering, so they will be working with trusted suppliers and vendors to create the new components.


The finished car will be much like a high-dollar restomod or elite custom build, in that it will have an upgraded and reinforced reproduction chassis, a powerful V-8 engine from GM’s LS family, and Wilwood brakes. Suspension will likely be Mustang II up front and C4 Corvette in the back. Hahn said that the GT Hawk’s interior will take after Stevens’ original design, with a padded cowl around the instrument panel, and some updates will include modern infotainment, technology, and comfort features. Since the cars will be commissioned, bespoke features are offered. Pricing has yet to be finalized.


Brooks Stevens, Inc.


What’s it going to be called? The trademark for the Studebaker brand is considered abandoned by the U.S. Patent & Trademark Office, and rights to some of the logos are retained by the Studebaker Museum and the Studebaker owners’ club, so I asked Hahn how they plan on branding the new/old Studebaker. He said that they hadn’t yet registered a trademark, but the project’s domain name is 65Hawk.com, so there’s a good chance the car will be badged with that in mind.


The allure of what could have been captivates fans of any product or company that no longer exists. Stevens’ Hawk sketches and the work of a few die-hards offer the rare chance to bring a dormant vision to fruition.
